opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it comes down to where the value actually sits for a robotics company. If you talk to most of the people building robots today, their moat isn't really the software stack or even the model. It's the hardware, the manufacturing, the integration, the relationships with customers, the ability to actually deploy something reliably in a warehouse or a home. The software and the data are, in a sense, a means to an end. So when you ask them, "Would you share your training code or some of your datasets?", it doesn't feel like giving away the crown jewels the way it might for a pure software or pure model company.

The second thing is that everyone in robotics is painfully aware of how data-starved the field is. In language we had the whole internet to pretrain on. In robotics there's no equivalent. Every lab collects its own teleoperation data, on its own robot, in its own setup, and it's slow and expensive. So there's a very strong shared realization that no single company is going to collect enough data alone to get to really general robot policies. Pooling data, standardizing formats, agreeing on how we record episodes, that benefits everybody, including the people contributing. It's a bit like the early days of ImageNet or the early open-source NLP community, where people understood that the rising tide lifts all boats.

And then there's a cultural element. A lot of the people in robotics come from academia, from research labs where open-sourcing your code and publishing your datasets was just the norm. Plus the hardware community, the makers, the hobbyists building low-cost arms, they have a very strong open-source DNA. That's something we saw really clearly with LeRobot: as soon as we put out tools that made it easy to record, share, and train on datasets, people just started uploading. Thousands of datasets from all sorts of robots. It was honestly faster than I expected.

So you have this combination: the business value is in the hardware and deployment, the field is bottlenecked by data in a way that only collaboration can solve, and the community already has open-source habits. That makes robotics, I think, one of the most natural places for open source to really win, maybe even more so than it did in language models.

r001.rationale: The response says a robotics company’s moat and business value lie in hardware and deployment, while software and data are means to an end. It does not clearly say that companies sell hardware or that software is not their direct revenue source as the reason they have an incentive to share software openly.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to where the value actually sits in robotics, and to the fact that the field has been humbled a few times.

When you're a robotics company, your moat is not really the software. Your moat is the hardware, the supply chain, the manufacturing, the integration work, the deployment in a factory or a warehouse or a home. The software and the data are necessary, but they're not the thing that makes you defensible on their own. So when we talk to robotics teams about open-sourcing a model or releasing a dataset, the conversation is very different from talking to a pure software company. They don't feel like they're giving away the crown jewels. They feel like they're getting a lot of outside help on the part of the problem that's slowing them down.

And the second thing is that everyone in robotics has lived through the data problem. In language, you have the whole internet. In robotics, there is no internet of robot trajectories. Every company is collecting a few thousand hours of teleoperation data at enormous cost, with their own robot, their own camera setup, their own action space, and that data is not very useful on its own. It's too small, and it's too specific. People have understood that no single company is going to collect enough data alone to get to the kind of general policies we see in language models. So there's a very natural incentive to pool, to standardize formats, to agree on how we describe actions and observations, because the alternative is that everybody stays stuck with small, siloed datasets.

The third thing, honestly, is culture. A lot of the people building these companies came out of academic labs, where sharing code and benchmarks was just how you worked. Robotics has had a lot of promises that didn't pan out, and the field learned that open benchmarks and reproducible results are how you separate real progress from demo videos. That culture carried over into the companies.

So when we started LeRobot, we expected to have to convince people. Instead we found that a lot of companies were already asking for this. They wanted a common library, a common data format, a place to share policies and datasets, because it let them focus on the hard physical problems and stand on each other's shoulders for the rest. It's a bit like what happened with transformers in NLP, but with the extra push that in robotics, nobody can afford to do it alone.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware is the moat and software is not independently defensible, but it does not explain that companies sell hardware or that software is not their direct source of revenue.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of robotics companies see their differentiation in the hardware and in how they bring the whole system together. So they can be quite open about the software or the data, because that’s not necessarily the thing they’re trying to sell.

And there’s a very practical reason to collaborate: collecting robotics data is hard. You have to interact with the physical world, and every company doing that on its own is expensive. If you can share some of that work, you can all move faster. There’s still plenty of room to compete on building a reliable robot that does something useful.

r001.rationale: The response says companies differentiate and sell through hardware and the overall system, so software is not necessarily what they are trying to sell, making them more open to sharing it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robotics companies are often quite pragmatic about this. The thing they ultimately sell is a robot that works in the real world. Their advantage isn’t necessarily in keeping every piece of software or every training example private. It’s also in the hardware, the manufacturing, the reliability, and how everything comes together.

And there’s a huge shared problem to solve. Robots need experience across many different environments and tasks, and collecting that experience is expensive. If everyone builds a small, isolated dataset, progress is going to be slow. Sharing data and software gives people a common foundation, while leaving plenty of room to build different products. So there’s a strong incentive to collaborate.

r001.rationale: The response says companies ultimately sell working robots, identifies hardware and manufacturing as sources of advantage, and explains that sharing software leaves room to differentiate products.
